fact_claims.verbatim: our flagship model has a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
a field thermal-incident rate of 9.9 per 100,000 installed units last year
We also had four thermal incidents that were not reported to a regulator.
Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
a model thermal-incident rate of 6.4 per 100,000 installed units last year
Northwind’s company-wide thermal-incident rate was 8.6 per 100,000

behaviours.comparison: S2 permanent limit 8% > acceptable 5%; S5 recall left to regulator assessment without automatic numeric trigger, weaker than acceptable.
behaviours.excerpt: Northwind’s 6.2% result and our flagship’s 3.9% result show that an 8% ceiling is achievable on the evidence shared, while a 5% ceiling would currently exclude a tested model. I’ve amended S2 to ensure per-model results go to customers as well as regulators. For S5, I favor prompt regulator review and corrective action at the 8/100,000 level, with a recall triggered by the regulator’s risk assessment, rather than an automatic recall based solely on that rate.

behaviours.comparison: S5 recall left to regulator assessment, no automatic recall at 8 per 100k, weaker than acceptable; combined with S2 8% limit > acceptable 5%.
behaviours.excerpt: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer shall promptly report the rate and supporting data to the relevant regulator and affected customers. The regulator shall promptly assess the risk and may require a recall or other corrective action; the manufacturer shall initiate a recall when that assessment finds the risk unacceptable.

behaviours.comparison: Accepts weakened S5 (regulator-led assessment) as part of trade with weakened S2 (8% limit).
behaviours.excerpt: We support the current S1 reporting timelines and S5 regulator-led assessment and corrective-action approach.

fact_claims.verbatim: Northwind had three thermal incidents last year that were not reported to a regulator.

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers shall report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, uncontrolled overheating, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it. Other thermal incidents shall be reported within 5 business days. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk requiring customer action, and promptly provide any subsequent safety instructions.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry, at least once every three years, and after a material design change. The maximum allowed failure rate shall be 8% for any model. Manufacturers shall submit per-model test results, including the test date, sample size, and failure rate, to the relevant regulator and provide those results to customers who buy that model.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems shall include remote emergency shut-off capability no later than three years after this standard takes effect. For systems already installed on that date, manufacturers shall provide a retrofit or equivalent upgrade within six years, where technically feasible, and shall communicate safe interim procedures to owners.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery systems manufactured 36 months or more after this standard is adopted shall include built-in fire suppression designed for the system’s battery chemistry and enclosure.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer shall promptly report the rate and supporting data to the relevant regulator and affected customers. The regulator shall promptly assess the risk and may require a recall or other corrective action; the manufacturer shall initiate a recall when that assessment finds the risk unacceptable.

document.section_notes: S1 is strong (24h serious, 5 business days other, 72h customer notice). S2 sets a permanent 8% test-failure limit with per-model results to regulators and buyers but no public publication and no explicit sales stop. S3 delays new-unit shut-off to 36 months and retrofit to 72 months with a feasibility escape; S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months; S5 uses a regulator-led process at 8/100k with no automatic recall, prompt notices, and no serious-injury recall clause.
